#4918. Bitcoin ETFs keep bleeding as BlackRock’s IBIT shares gain nearly 5%

BlackRock’s IBIT shares gained 4.85% on Monday despite continued Bitcoin ETF withdrawals that pushed November’s net outflows to $4.71 billion.

US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) extended their outflow streak to five consecutive trading days amid a rebound in shares of the largest Bitcoin fund, BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT).

The funds recorded $569.7 million in net outflows on Monday, bringing November’s total so far to $4.71 billion, according to SoSoValue data. The withdrawals have surpassed June’s record of $4.51 billion, putting the funds on track for their worst month since launching in January 2024.

IBIT shares gained 4.85% on Monday to close at $34.62 before slipping 1.3% in overnight trading, Yahoo Finance data showed. Meanwhile, Bitcoin (BTC) fell 1.8% over 24 hours to around $60,450, erasing Monday’s rally following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded $2.37 billion in net outflows over the past five trading sessions, led by IBIT’s $1.95 billion in withdrawals. The BlackRock fund broke its daily outflow record twice last week.

Bitwise’s Camran Khosravi attributed IBIT’s record outflows to a broader retreat from risk assets amid tech and artificial intelligence sector concerns and hawkish Federal Reserve signals.

“The largest funds naturally see the largest flows in both directions, and even record daily outflows are small relative to their total assets,” Khosravi told Cointelegraph.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs held $73.6 billion in combined net assets as of Monday, with IBIT holding $45.64 billion, according to WalletPilot data.

Kraken parent Payward's money app Krak has opened a waitlist for two U.S. credit cards, including one that lets customers use USDC as collateral while earning yield, according to a statement shared exclusively with The Block.

The Krak Credit Card and Krak Secured Card are expected to begin shipping in early 2027. Both offer up to 4% cashback in either dollars or bitcoin once a purchase settles, with rewards paid directly into customers' Krak accounts rather than issued as points.

Payward considers the cashback as part of its wider relationship with customers rather than treating the cards as standalone products, a company spokesperson told The Block. The company earns revenue from card payments, assets customers hold with it, and other everyday uses of Krak, they said.

A national survey of 2,001 U.S. adults commissioned by Krak and conducted by Morning Consult in July found that 30% of Americans do not own a credit card. Nearly two-thirds said they were frustrated with existing credit card rewards programs, while 57% preferred cash rewards over points.

"Credit is fundamental to financial opportunity in America, yet the credit card industry has spent decades pouring resources into increasingly complex rewards schemes instead of focusing on making credit products more accessible," Payward co-CEO Arjun Sethi said on Tuesday. "The result is a system that remains outdated, fragmented and out of reach for millions of people."

Krak is offering the standard card to eligible customers with established credit histories. The secured card is designed for people building or rebuilding their credit, including crypto-native customers whose wealth is primarily held outside the traditional banking system, the firm said. Krak does not guarantee that using the card will establish or improve a customer's credit score.

For the secured card, users can deposit between $350 and $5,000 in USDC, depending on their desired credit limit, the spokesperson said. The USDC remains in their Krak accounts as collateral and can earn up to 4% APY through Krakpass, while cardholders can also receive up to 4% cashback on purchases, according to the firm.

The cards also include access to Visa Signature experiences, protections, and other benefits that are offered via the Visa network, the firm said.

Krak's card lineup already includes a U.S. debit card, alongside personal accounts for cash and digital assets in the same app. Payward introduced its U.S. Krak Debit Cards earlier this year, following a UK and EU rollout of Krak debit cards, salary deposits, and new wealth tools that began in November 2025. It had launched the Krak app five months earlier in June 2025 as a rival to Venmo and PayPal. The company said Tuesday that its debit-card offering has surpassed 200,000 cardholders globally.

Payward previously disclosed plans to test a U.S. credit card in its third-quarter update earlier this month, alongside plans to settle U.S. dollar wires through its Federal Reserve master account and to fund lending in Europe with customer deposits. Payward reported $60 million in Q3 adjusted EBITDA, up from $23 million in the second quarter, but down from the $178.6 million it posted a year earlier.

Both of the U.S. credit cards require Krakpass, which costs $6.29 per month when billed annually or is free for customers with more than $3,000 in monthly direct deposits, the firm said. Payward has not yet disclosed the cards' APRs or fees, with full program terms due before issuance.

First Electronic Bank will issue the cards under a license from Visa U.S.A. The cards will be offered through Kraken and Cardless. Cardless, a fintech that provides technology and servicing for branded credit card programs, will also handle program management, technology, and servicing.

Payward said the cards will not be available in all U.S. states and that it plans to introduce similar offerings in additional markets globally over the following year.

#4916. Justice Department Moves to Forfeit $1.1B in USDC From North Korea's Binance Hack

Justice Department Moves to Forfeit $1.1B in USDC From North Korea's Binance Hack

The U.S. Justice Department has moved to permanently take control of more than $1.1 billion in crypto stolen by North Korean hackers in the record $6.4 billion theft from Binance.

The department filed a civil forfeiture claim on Monday for the funds, which are held in USDC, the stablecoin issued by Circle, it said. The assets were already subject to a restraining order the government had requested after the hack, and Circle provided "valuable assistance," the department said.

The filing is part of a wider U.S. effort to help Binance recover the stolen funds. Since the October 29 hack, the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in crypto, according to the department. That is up from the $2.7 billion in frozen assets it reported on November 12, when it said it had court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion.

"Swift coordination between the government and private sector partners helped prevent a substantial portion of those assets from disappearing," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the department's Criminal Division said in a statement.

Secret Service investigators identified and froze stolen funds "within minutes of the hack," said Todd Bratz, special agent in charge of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. The Secret Service is investigating the case alongside the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation.

The FBI has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, which the Justice Department describes as members of the North Korean military. North Korea has denied involvement, and Binance has set aside $6.34 billion to cover customer losses.

Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze funds after the hack. But the hackers have kept moving what they still control. After two weeks of inactivity, wallets tied to the hack began moving Ethereum in mid-November.

At least $247 million has since been funneled through Bitcoin coinjoins, a mixing technique that pools funds to obscure their origin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said on Monday. Elliptic estimates that about $2.85 billion has been frozen and that roughly $2.35 billion remains in addresses tied to the theft.

Binance has also pursued the funds through the courts, winning a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts that can be served on wallet holders via the blockchain.

On Tuesday, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance said it would not recommend charges to the Commission regarding Molecule's project tokens.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's staff said it would not recommend an enforcement action against decentralized science infrastructure company Molecule for its utility tokens that allow people to support scientific research.

On Tuesday, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance said it would not recommend charges to the Commission regarding Molecule's project tokens.

"Based on the facts presented, the Division will not recommend enforcement action to the Commission if, in reliance on your opinion as counsel, LabsCo offers and sells Project Tokens in the manner and under the circumstances described in your letter without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act and does not register Project Tokens as a class of equity securities under Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act," the SEC said in a statement.

This comes after lawyers representing Molecule sent a letter to the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance last week asking for relief. The agency has issued several crypto-related no-action letters over the past year amid its friendlier regulatory stance, including for DoubleZero, Fuse and more recently, Canton.

In the letter, the lawyers refer to a coin-to-company model, Molecule's framework that allows users to receive tokens and then gain equity ownership in science projects they support. They refer to the Howey Test — a 1946 U.S. Supreme Court case to determine if an asset qualifies as an investment contract and, therefore, a security — and say the token fails to satisfy it in part because it does not have an expectation of profit derived from the effort of others.

Molecule said its first project in the ecosystem will use coin-to-company in the next few weeks.

"The Coin-to-Company No Action Letter brings together the best of blockchains with traditional equity structures to accelerate the production and commercialization of science in the US, Europe and worldwide," said Molecule Chief Legal Officer Benjamin Snipes, in a post from the company on X.

#4908. South Korea proposes bank-led stablecoins, 20% cap on crypto exchange stakes

The draft bill would also reopen domestic initial coin offerings after a ban dating to 2017 and require issuers to disclose risks before soliciting buyers.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) unveiled a draft bill Tuesday that would initially limit issuance of won-denominated stablecoins to groups majority-owned by banks and generally cap shareholders’ stakes in crypto exchanges at 20%.

Banks would have to own more than half of a stablecoin issuer collectively, though a fintech or technology company could be its largest individual shareholder, the FSC said in its announcement.

Domestic stablecoin issuers would need FSC authorization and at least 5 billion won (about $3.7 million) in equity capital. They would also have to hold reserves covering at least 100% of their outstanding tokens and redeem them at face value without delay.

Exchanges would need dealing, brokerage and custody licenses and would have to meet capital and operating requirements. Shareholders’ stakes would be capped at 20%, or 34% with FSC approval.

The draft also seeks to lift South Korea’s 2017 ban on domestic initial coin offerings.

Regulators previously aimed to produce the bill in 2025, the year President Lee Jae-myung campaigned on introducing a won-denominated stablecoin.

Work stalled over who could issue the tokens. The central bank wanted banks to control issuers, while the FSC favored allowing nonbank companies to issue them as well. The proposed cap on exchange ownership also drew opposition from lawmakers.

#4907. Europol Traces $28M in Crypto Behind Europe's Illegal Streaming Industry

Europol Traces $28M in Crypto Behind Europe's Illegal Streaming Industry

Law enforcement agencies from 11 countries have traced more than €26 million ($28 million) in crypto payments linked to illegal TV streaming services, in an operation that brought in crypto exchanges Binance and Coinbase and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, Europol said on Tuesday.

The five-day operation, held at the Spanish National Police headquarters in Seville from November 16 to November 20, 2026, disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services. Investigators also identified 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, which together receive more than 7.3 million visits a year. Analysis of the crypto transactions is continuing.

Investigators are increasingly targeting the money behind illegal streaming services, not just the services themselves.

Last week, Chainalysis joined Europol, law enforcement from 11 countries, and industry partners including Binance and Coinbase in Seville for a five-day… pic.twitter.com/XqV0Hima26

— Chainalysis (@chainalysis) November 24, 2026

IPTV, or internet protocol television, services sell access to television channels, live sports and films over the internet. Illegal providers charge a few euros a month for unauthorized access to premium content, often taking subscription payments in crypto, according to Europol.

During the operation, investigators traced suspicious transactions across blockchains to find links between illegal services, the crypto wallets receiving payments and the people controlling them.

Europol said the operation reflected a shift in strategy. Rather than focusing only on shutting down streaming services, investigators are increasingly targeting the financial infrastructure behind them, because taking a service offline does not necessarily stop the people running it.

Europol has gone after criminals' crypto in other cases, too. In June 2026, its Operation Endgame froze more than €41 million ($47 million) in crypto linked to infostealer malware, and in March it helped disrupt a proxy network whose payment platform had received more than $5.7 million in crypto.

Around 40 people took part, including 30 law enforcement officers from Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Spain and the U.S.

Europol coordinated the operation through its Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition, a unit supported by the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), which also took part alongside INTERPOL and the Audio-visual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA). The information gathered will feed into national investigations to identify suspects and trace assets.

An estimated 60 million people in Europe use unauthorized IPTV services, costing legitimate providers €4.83 billion ($5.3 billion) a year and governments a further €1.08 billion ($1.2 billion) in lost taxes, according to AAPA figures cited by Europol. Demand appears to be growing: visits to websites offering sign-ups for illegal IPTV services rose 10% in 2023, an EUIPO study found.

Europol ran a similar operation last year. In November 2025, a week-long cyber-patrol in Alicante, Spain, traced about $55 million in crypto linked to piracy services and referred 25 illegal IPTV services to crypto providers for disruption, The Record reported at the time.

Crypto also features in older piracy cases. In Germany, the alleged operator of defunct piracy site Movie2K has been offered a deal to end his money laundering and tax evasion trial if he hands over 40,000 BTC. Prosecutors believe he still holds about 56,000 BTC, bought with proceeds from the site before it shut down in 2013.

The offer came days after German lawmakers approved new powers allowing customs officials to seize crypto and other assets of unclear origin without first opening a criminal case.

Ansem Meme Coin Crashes After $2.57 Million Wallet Drain, Bullpen Confirms Security Breach

Crypto trading platform Bullpen confirmed a security incident on Tuesday after a wallet belonging to popular crypto influencer Ansem dumped millions of dollars worth of meme coins, which led to accusations that the trader had deliberately sold his holdings and blamed hackers.

The incident sent The Black Bull, a Solana meme coin that trades as ANSEM named after the influencer, crashing roughly 60% in less than an hour. An on-chain investigation subsequently identified $2.57 million in funds transferred to a wallet on Arbitrum.

“On November 24, we identified unauthorized transfers involving Bullpen accounts opened during our early beta between April and June 2024,” the company said on X. “Our preliminary count is 18–19 affected accounts, including [Ansem’s].”

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Solana with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The announcement lends credibility to Ansem's explanation of what happened earlier Tuesday, when blockchain trackers spotted his wallet rapidly liquidating its meme coin holdings.

“Pump wallet is hacked, trying to figure out how, believe its unauthorized access to my bullpen profile somehow which had the sol priv key imported,” Ansem wrote on X.

Bullpen, a crypto trading terminal co-founded by Ansem himself, allows traders to import existing wallets using their private keys. Anyone who obtains that key can effectively take control of the corresponding wallet, signing transactions that the blockchain recognizes as legitimate regardless of who initiated them.

A subsequent investigation by blockchain data provider Bitquery identified moved funds at $2.57 million total, with approximately $2.1 million coming from meme coin sales.

Ansem's explanation initially met considerable skepticism from crypto traders and blockchain researchers, some of whom pointed to what appeared to be connections between the recipient wallet and the influencer's older addresses.

“Pretty sure Ansem didn’t get hacked lol,” pseudonymous blockchain researcher MLM wrote on X.

“The onchain activity looks nothing like a hack,” he added. “Just an hour before the selling started, a previously inactive wallet I’d labeled as Ansem’s a year ago funded the wallet that later received the sale proceeds.”

A proposed Community Note on Ansem's post went considerably further, accusing the influencer of deliberately liquidating his position and transferring the proceeds to his own wallets. The note even drew a comparison with Haliey Welch, the internet celebrity behind the controversial HAWK meme coin.

The note was still awaiting additional ratings.

Ansem rose to prominence during the 2024 meme coin frenzy thanks in part to his calls on tokens such as Dogwifhat (WIF). Decrypt named him among its rising crypto stars that year, when his following had grown to approximately 600,000 accounts on X.

His namesake token debuted on the Solana meme coin factory Pump.fun in June 2026 after an anonymous developer created the coin and allocated a substantial portion of its supply to the influencer.

There were also reasons to question the accusations against Ansem before Bullpen issued its statement. Bitquery found that an older Solana wallet was emptied around the same time as his main wallet, potentially explaining why an address previously associated with the trader had funded the recipient.

Meanwhile, his Hyperliquid trading account, which held approximately $373,000, remained untouched. Someone with access exclusively to his Solana private keys would not necessarily have access to that account.

Bullpen said the affected accounts represent less than 0.005% of its registered user base. The company has yet to disclose the precise vulnerability, the total losses across affected accounts, or whether it intends to compensate users.

“We’ve taken the affected test service offline,” Bullpen said, adding that it would contact affected users directly and provide updates every three hours throughout the investigation.

#4898. I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

Plus, the expert-backed reason a few minutes of mobility can add up over time.

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, says Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

“Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance issues, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”

That’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

Mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” says Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”

And just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he says.

My routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

During the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

From the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

Heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

By the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

That said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

However, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”

Kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

Following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

#4897. What Is Pons? The Robinhood Chain Meme Coin Launchpad Explained

What Is Pons? The Robinhood Chain Meme Coin Launchpad Explained

When Robinhood switched on its own Robinhood Chain blockchain on July 1, 2026, the trading app's stock tokens were supposed to be the main attraction. Instead, much of the early activity came from meme coins: tokens built around a joke or an internet trend.

Pons became the busiest place to make them. Like Pump.fun on Solana, it lets anyone pick a name, ticker and image and have a tradable token minutes later, without writing code. Its fees briefly made it one of the highest-earning protocols in crypto, and its own token, PONS, went on to list on Kraken and Coinbase.

That openness can also be exploited. In September 2026, an onchain analyst alleged that one group had used Pons launches to extract millions of dollars from buyers.

This guide explains what Pons is, how its two generations of contracts work, what the PONS token does, and the risks.

Pons is a token launch protocol running on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 network built on Ethereum using Arbitrum's technology, and its website and documentation are published by Pons Labs, LLC.

Every token launched through Pons is a standard ERC-20 token with a fixed supply, 1 billion tokens on V1 launches, that can never be increased. The creator gets no allocation set aside before trading opens.

Pons is also non-custodial. Its documentation says every launch and trade is a transaction the user's own wallet signs, and the platform never holds user funds.

Pons went live within days of Robinhood Chain's mainnet. It picked up most of the chain's launchpad activity after an early rival, Noxa, stopped accepting new launches on July 11, 2026, according to Decrypt's reporting.

Pons has two generations of contracts, V1 and V2, and both remain live on Robinhood Chain.

In V1, a single transaction deploys the token and its trading pool, a Uniswap V3 pool paired with wrapped ETH (WETH), and locks the pool's liquidity so the creator can't withdraw it. Each launch costs 0.0005 ETH and carries a 1% trading fee, the documentation says. A launch "graduates" once 4.2 ETH has been paired in its pool by default, but trading carries on in the same pool.

V1 launches are protected for their first two blocks: in the launch block, only the creator's initial buy can execute, and for the rest of the window no wallet can hold more than 5% of supply or buy more than 5.5%. Fees are split 70% to the creator and 30% to the protocol for current launches.

V2 adds a bonding curve: a contract that holds a token's whole supply and sets its price by formula, rising as people buy and falling as they sell. According to the V2 documentation, the curve sells out, then "graduates" automatically into a Uniswap V4 pool, seeded with a fixed share of supply held back from the start. The pool's liquidity is then locked permanently; no unlock function exists.

V2 launches can be priced in ETH or in other assets Pons has approved, including tokenized stocks, in which case the creator is paid in that asset. Each trade pays a standard fee shared between Pons, the creator and an optional buyback, plus an optional creator tax that is capped by the protocol and fixed at launch.

When a creator turns buybacks on, part of their own fee is spent buying their token back. Those tokens are locked in a vault and released over five years, split between the creator and the protocol.

PONS itself was launched through Pons's own legacy V1 factory, and its documentation uses PONS as the reference token for developers testing their integrations.

"Sniping" means buying a large share of a new token in its first seconds, often with bots, then selling into later buyers. Every V2 launch opens with a "snipe tax" of 99% on buys that decays to zero over five seconds, the documentation says.

The launching wallet and the creator's fee wallet are exempt automatically, and creators can name up to 32 more exempt addresses at launch "for a team bundling its opening buys across several wallets."

That exemption became central to allegations published on September 27, 2026. Pseudonymous onchain analyst Wazz tweeted that a single operation had extracted at least $18.43 million from 53 Robinhood Chain launches between July 10 and September 21, 2026, mostly through Pons V2. Wazz said nearly every launch was sniped for 70% or more of its supply by bundles of 70 to 200 wallets.

I just uncovered the biggest serial Rugpulling and Extraction operation on Robinhood

The same operation is linked 53 launches within a 2 month period

very likely more this is just what I could directly link

🧵 https://t.co/wS62KAbvv5 pic.twitter.com/BSxZL9wU44

The Block reviewed the onchain data and found that creators of nine Pons V2 launches had exempted 15 to 25 wallets each from the snipe tax, which then bought out the bonding curve in a single transaction. The creator and those wallets held 82% to 86% of supply after the opening buys. The Block did not independently replicate Wazz's $18.43 million total.

On September 3, 2026, Pons generated $5.95 million in daily fees, briefly out-earning Robinhood Chain itself and ranking fourth among all protocols tracked by DefiLlama, Decrypt reported. Pons fees drove Robinhood Chain to a record of about $6 million in daily fees in early September 2026, The Block reported.

On September 5, 2026, blockchain analytics firm Arkham tweeted that crypto market maker Wintermute appeared to be buying PONS slowly in a series of small purchases, and held just over $3 million of the token. Wallets that Arkham attributes to Wintermute held about 3.4 million PONS at the time, and about 7.4 million as of November 2026.

As of November 20, 2026, DefiLlama put Pons's cumulative fees at about $205 million. Of that, $137 million came in September 2026 alone; fees fell to about $17 million in October 2026.

PONS is the ERC-20 token tied to the Pons launchpad, with a fixed supply of 1 billion. Its link to the platform is a buyback.

According to the V1 documentation, 80% of the protocol's fees are used to buy PONS on the market through an automated process and send it to a burn address, permanently removing it from circulation. The remaining 20% pays for infrastructure and the Pons team. Kraken's listing notice describes the same mechanism.

As of November 20, 2026, CoinGecko data shows about 669 million PONS in circulation, out of a fixed supply of 1 billion.

You can track PONS's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

PONS trades in Uniswap pools on Robinhood Chain. Binance Wallet added it to its Binance Alpha tier on September 2, 2026, and Kraken opened PONS trading on September 25, 2026, with access through the Kraken App and Instant Buy to follow once liquidity allows. Coinbase Markets tweeted on October 6, 2026, that it had added PONS to its listing roadmap, and said the next day that its PONS-USD pair would open later that day, if liquidity conditions were met.

Pons has flagged several changes still to come. Its V1 documentation says the 80% share of protocol fees used to buy back PONS is not yet fixed in its contracts, but will become "immutable, decentralized, and automated" in a future release.

On V2, three security firms (SB Security, Dingbats and Pashov Audit Group) are reviewing the contracts, and Pons says it will publish their reports in full, including any findings it did not accept, once the reviews close. Until then, its documentation tells users to treat V2 as unaudited, and only whitelisted addresses can create V2 tokens.

Pons also faces competition on its home chain. Uniswap, already Robinhood Chain's main exchange, launched its own launchpad, Pools.trade, on August 5, 2026. It charges no launchpad fee, locks each launch's liquidity permanently, and offers a "crowd launch" option designed to resist bundling. Within its first days, Pools.trade took about half of Robinhood Chain's launchpad volume, Decrypt's Morning Minute newsletter reported. The newsletter noted that Uniswap can afford to forgo launchpad fees because it earns from its other products, which most dedicated launchpads cannot.

Pons has since kept the larger share of fees. As of November 2026, DefiLlama showed Pons collecting about $5.6 million in fees over the previous 30 days, against about $115,000 for Pools.trade. The two charge different rates, though: Pools.trade's trading fee is 0.25%, while Pons's standard fee is 1%.

V2's tokenized-stock pairs link Pons launches to the stock tokens Robinhood built the chain to carry, which ties Pons's prospects to Robinhood Chain itself. On Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call on October 27, 2026, CEO Vlad Tenev said the growth of the chain and its ecosystem had exceeded the company's expectations, and that Robinhood was investing in how to support the chain's developer community.

#4895. Swiss central bank, UBS and SIX study ledger for tokenized settlement

The study will assess whether a shared ledger can bring central bank money, commercial bank money and securities onto the same platform.

The Swiss National Bank (SNB), UBS, SIX and other financial institutions announced a study Tuesday into whether a shared ledger could settle domestic and cross-border transactions involving tokenized assets.

Other participants include Zürcher Kantonalbank, PostFinance, Banque Cantonale Vaudoise, Basler Kantonalbank, Sygnum Bank and settlement platform Seturion, the central bank said in its announcement.

The proposed Swiss Financial Ledger would bring central bank money, commercial bank money and securities onto one platform. Participants will assess the benefits and risks, compare designs and examine how to govern and operate the ledger. The SNB said the study leaves open whether the ledger will launch or the central bank will issue tokenized money to financial institutions.

The initiative is part of the SNB’s Project Helvetia, which explores how to settle tokenized asset transactions in central bank money.

It also builds on Project Agorá, an initiative of the Bank for International Settlements and the Institute of International Finance, which explores whether tokenization can make wholesale cross-border payments faster, cheaper and safer.

#4893. Get the Women’s Health Beginner Workout Plan: 4-Week Strength Training and Cardio Program

It’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately. My feed is full of people hitting the weights for the first time ever or setting big goals like getting their first pull-up. And let me just say: It’s awesome!

So, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party. When you’re starting to work out, it can be hard to sift through all the options and find a program that’s actually accessible for a true beginner (or, someone restarting after quite some time). That is, until now.

The Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey. This comprehensive program guides you through strength and cardio workouts that only take between 20 and 45 minutes. And, of course, it answers every burning question you could have about starting a fitness routine.

No matter your age or experience, starting an exercise routine has many benefits, says Kristen McParland, CPT, your coach for the next four weeks. Building muscle increases total-body strength; your bones, ligaments, and tendons get healthier; and even your blood pressure and immunity may improve. So lace up those sneakers and we’ll see you at the gym now, too.

Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan

Over the next four weeks, you’ll follow a specific plan each day, focusing either on strength training, optional cardio, active recovery, or rest (more on these, below). Each strength workout includes a warm-up and a cooldown (which you can use on cardio days, too). More info on each below.

Simply follow the instructions of each full-body strength training workout in the Women's Health+ Beginner Workout Plan. You can find detailed how-to instructions for each exercise in the Exercise Guide section of the PDF.

Equipment Needed: Dumbbells, kettlebells, a step or box, and a slam ball. Don’t have access to a kettlebell or slam ball? Don't worry—you can still do those exercises with a dumbbell.

Cardio is important for everyone, regardless of fitness level or routine. That’s because when you’re lifting heavy, your heart needs to be able to take on that stress. Training cardio—through running, cycling, or brisk walking—will help improve your heart strength.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Complete 20 to 30 minutes of running, biking, cycling, rowing, or using the elliptical or stair climber (whatever you enjoy). No matter which form of cardio you choose, start with interval training: exert yourself for 30 seconds, then go at a light pace for 1 to 2 minutes, alternating the pattern for a total of 20 minutes. The goal is to “get your heart rate up, but then pull it back and recover,” McParland says. Eventually, you’ll be able to decrease the rest time and maintain that higher-intensity movement for 15 to 20 minutes without a break.

Your activity on this day is up to you. The goal is to do some kind of low-intensity movement lasting 20 minutes. Some ideas: outdoor walk or hike, bike ride, incline treadmill walk, yoga, or Pilates class.

Take this day to relax so your muscles have time to repair. Still, if your body is craving some type of activity for recovery, you could stretch, go for a walk, or even try a treatment like a massage, sauna, or cold-plunge session.

Here’s how things will progress each week.

Complete the five programmed workouts when it’s convenient for you. Focus on your form and take your two rest days when you need to recover.

If you completed all the workouts in Week 1, repeat them during Week 2, adjusting one variable in your routine, McParland says: the number of reps or sets, the weight, the speed of the moves (slower is harder). If you missed a workout, don’t stress. Refocus on completing all of the Week 1 workouts before making any of the changes above.

You’ve officially done two full weeks of this workout plan—nice job! During this third week, repeat the workouts from Week 2 in exactly the same way or adjust one variable again (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, and rest periods). If you feel you’re crushing it and are ready to level up, try the third full-body strength workout.

Still going strong? Thought so! Hit all six workouts and adjust one variable per workout for an extra challenge (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, rest time). You can also ramp up your cardio time (to 30 to 40 minutes) or speed, shorten rest intervals (for interval training), or raise your step goal by 10 percent (e.g., if your daily step goal was 5,000 a day, make it 5,500).

Ready to become your strongest self? Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan now.

When you’re just beginning to work out, do a minimum of two full-body strength training days each week, McParland recommends. During both of those days, you should hit at least one exercise from each category of the foundational movement patterns. This will give you enough of a challenge to stimulate muscle growth, she says.

During the first two weeks of this plan, you will have two strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will 20 to 30 minutes), one day of active rest (a stint of low-intensity movement lasting at least 20 minutes), and two recovery days, for a total of five workouts per week.

After those two weeks, see how your body feels and if your body is craving a third day of full-body training. If so, progress to the next phase of this plan. That weekly schedule consists of three strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will run 20 to 30 minutes), one active rest day (lasting at least 20 minutes), and one recovery day, for a total of six workouts per week. If your body isn’t ready for three strength-training days yet, wait another two weeks. Once you’ve completed the full four weeks of this plan, consider adding in the third day.

Start with medium weights that will challenge you for 10 to 12 reps, says Sariya. Essentially, you’ll want to feel you’ve reached 70 to 80 percent of your rate of perceived exertion (i.e., your fatigue level is at a 7 or 8 out of 10) by the time you’re doing your final reps in a set. When you feel you can do more than 12 reps, it’s time to increase your weight, but keep the same number of reps. This way, you’re always working toward your goal of building strength.

As for how much to increase by: a good rule of thumb is 2.5 to 5 pounds for an upper-body exercise and 5 to 10 pounds for a lower-body move.

What if I need to rest in the middle of a set?

Resting during a workout is important—if you don’t take enough time to recover between exercises, you won’t have enough energy in your body for the next one. With this plan, you’ll rest between moves in a superset or tri-set for 20 to 30 seconds, or however long it takes to transition between exercises. Between supersets and tri-sets, you’ll rest for one minute.

If you get fatigued in the middle of a set, push through if you feel safe doing so, Sariya says. However, if you feel dizzy or fear you might drop a weight on yourself, put it down and take time to recover. When you’re feeling better, you can start again. If you’re in any sort of pain, stop the workout entirely.

Cardio is a great supplement to strength training, McParland says. Plus, it has a slew of benefits, such as better endurance in strength training, better blood pressure regulation, and higher VO2 max, she says.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Pick any form of cardio you enjoy, whether that’s brisk walking, running, cycling, or swimming, and sprinkle it in two or three days a week for 20 to 30 minutes, McParland recommends.

On an active rest day, you’ll still exercise a bit through low-intensity movement, like a leisurely bike ride or hike. On a recovery day, you’ll do just that: recover. After all, you need to give your muscles time to rebuild and repair, Sariya says. But to maximize the recovery aspect, you can also opt to stretch, go for a gentle walk, or even get a self-care body treatment like a massage.

Once you’ve got the WH+ Beginner Workout Plan under your belt, you’re ready to take things to another level. One way to do that is by simply restarting the program—and completing the moves with heavier weights this time. (This is called progressive overload, and it’s another foundational concept in strength training. The idea is that over time, you will keep increasing the stimulus to your muscles to continuously challenge them and make them stronger.)

Picking the right weight is an art as much as it is a science, but for a general rule of thumb, for upper-body moves, increase your weights by 2.5 to 5 pounds and see how that feels. For lower-body ones, try adding 5 to 10. You should feel like you’re ending each set two to three reps away from failure (where your form starts to break down). You can tell you’re close if your range of motion starts to shorten or your reps are slowing down. That’s how you know you’re successfully challenging yourself. And, if you don’t happen to have a lot of different-sized weights at your disposal, you can always just increase the number of reps you do instead.

But, if you’re looking for something new, WH+ has a bunch of other trainer-created programs to help you grow your knowledge and confidence in the gym and attack other fitness goals.

#4892. USDT buyers face 22% VAT when Moscow Exchange opens crypto trading

Buyers will pay VAT on top of the trade price in December because Russia’s tax code has no explicit exemption for foreign digital instruments.

Buyers of Tether’s USDt (USDT) stablecoin will pay a 22% value-added tax (VAT) on top of the trade price when Moscow Exchange (MOEX) opens crypto trading on Dec. 1, according to the exchange’s clearinghouse.

The National Clearing Centre (NCC) said it would apply VAT to USDT purchases, sales and swaps through Dec. 31. A buyer purchasing 100,000 rubles worth of USDT would pay an additional 22,000 rubles in VAT.

Unlike Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH), which Russia classifies as digital currencies, USDT falls under a separate legal category known as foreign digital instruments. Russia’s tax code excludes sales of digital currencies from VAT, but it provides no explicit exemption for foreign digital instruments, according to the NCC.

The NCC said it had asked Russia’s Federal Tax Service and Finance Ministry for guidance. It said it would update market participants if it received clarification or if lawmakers exempted trades conducted before Jan. 1, 2027.

Bank of Russia rules that took effect Nov. 17 allow non-qualified investors to buy Bitcoin, Ether and USDT through intermediaries, with annual purchases capped at 300,000 rubles (about $3,650) per intermediary.

#4891. Wall Street and Crypto Are in 'Extreme Fear'. What's Spooking Investors?

Wall Street and Crypto Are in 'Extreme Fear'. What's Spooking Investors?

Investors in both the stock and cryptocurrency markets are back in panic mode Tuesday, just one day after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO triggered a massive rally across risk assets.

Bitcoin is trading at around $59,500, down 2.74% since the daily session opened, while the total cryptocurrency market capitalization has fallen 4.44% to $2.04 trillion, per CoinMarketCap. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 are also in the red, giving back some of Monday's gains.

CoinMarketCap's Fear and Greed Index (which tracks the sentiment across all the crypto market) currently sits at 9 out of 100, matching Friday's reading, the lowest since February. Just three months ago, the same indicator reached its yearly high of 82, corresponding to extreme greed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Over on Wall Street, CNN's equivalent sits at 17, also in extreme fear territory, after reaching its lowest level since March on Friday.

Both indexes measure investor sentiment on a scale from zero to 100, with lower readings indicating greater fear. They use different methodologies, incorporating market momentum, volatility, and trading behavior rather than simply asking investors how they feel.

The artificial intelligence industry, largely responsible for Wall Street's extraordinary performance over the past few years, is now at the center of the selloff.

Last week, the Nasdaq lost approximately 10%, its worst weekly performance since 2020, wiping out its gains for the year. The S&P 500 entered correction territory, having fallen more than 10% from its October peak.

Nvidia's leadership crisis made things considerably worse. The world's leading AI chipmaker had lost nearly half its market value from its October highs before the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday, sending its shares up 31.5% by the closing bell.

But having Huang back at Nvidia doesn't necessarily make AI investments more profitable.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure will generate enough revenue to justify the expense. As Decrypt previously reported, 52% of respondents to Bank of America's November fund manager survey expect at least one major cloud computing company to announce spending cuts within six months.

Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO hasn't helped much, either. Shares of the Claude developer fell below their $83 offering price Tuesday, less than a week after the company made its stock market debut at $111.50.

Nvidia fell 5.8% during early trading Tuesday, while AI infrastructure providers CoreWeave and IREN lost 6.9% and 9%, respectively. Healthcare and consumer staples stocks were doing considerably better, suggesting investors are moving money into businesses less dependent on the AI boom.

An additional concern for both markets is that the U.S. Federal Reserve could make money more expensive at precisely the moment the AI industry needs more of it.

Traders are pricing in a 98% probability of a December interest rate hike and a 66% chance of another increase in January, according to CME FedWatch data.

Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for companies building data centers and reduce the present value of their expected future profits. They also make government bonds more attractive relative to speculative assets such as Bitcoin, which doesn't generate income for its holders.

For crypto investors, this comes at a particularly bad time.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded another $569.7 million in net withdrawals on Monday, despite Bitcoin's brief recovery, per Decrypt’s ETF tracker. BlackRock's IBIT alone accounted for $509.3 million.

November's cumulative Bitcoin ETF outflows have now reached $4.71 billion, surpassing June's previous monthly record with four trading sessions still remaining.

Bitcoin's daily chart shows a cryptocurrency struggling to hold a price range that has served as support on several occasions since 2024.

BTC has lost approximately 53% of its value from its October 2025 all-time high, and the recovery that took Bitcoin above $85,000 in September has largely evaporated.

The $60,000 area is particularly relevant because buyers stepped in around similar prices in February and June. Friday's dip toward $55,000 established another potential support area, with historical buying activity around $50,000 further below.

Extreme fear readings have historically coincided with some attractive buying opportunities, but they are notoriously unreliable at identifying the exact bottom. Bitcoin can remain oversold for extended periods, particularly when institutional investors are pulling billions of dollars out of the market.

Investors will get another important piece of economic data Wednesday, when the U.S. releases its Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation report, the Fed's preferred measure of inflation and the last major data release before its December monetary policy meeting.

#4889. The Best Lymphatic Drainage Tools in 2026

These may help to de-puff your face and body.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You've seen enough GRWM videos to know that plenty of people are incorporating lymphatic drainage tools into their morning routines. If you also grapple with regular facial puffiness, it's fair to wonder if lymphatic drainage tools could help.

These tools are marketed to encourage the flow of lymph, which is a clear, watery fluid that supports fluid balance and immune defenses in your body. The idea with lymphatic drainage tools—which include gua sha stones, facial rollers, dry brushes, and more—is to mechanically encourage the movement of lymphatic fluid to reduce puffiness and fluid retention.

Dermatologists say there's something to this. "Your lymph system helps move excess waste and fluid throughout the body," explains Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research at Mount Sinai Hospital. "Lymphatic massages help enhance activity of the system to circulate excess fluid and depuff."

Doctors may recommend lymphatic drainage massage to people with health conditions like lymphedema or to post-surgical patients, says Ife J. Rodney, MD, founding director of Eternal Dermatology + Aesthetics. For everyone else, the data is less clear on whether lymphatic drainage offers much benefit.

"For everyday facial puffiness, gentle massage may offer temporary improvement, though research on gua sha is limited," Dr. Rodney says. Note the "temporary" part of what she said. Despite what you may hear on social media, lymphatic drainage won't permanently alter your cheekbones and jawline, although Dr. Rodney says this may help your skin look fresher and your features look more defined. "Think of it as an optional self-care step, not a requirement for healthy skin," Dr. Rodney says.

Want to opt into this? There is a range of tools to consider—and doctors say you don't need to spend a ton to get results.

A gua sha tool needs to have at least one smooth edge for lymphatic drainage. But Face Gym's Multi-Sculpt High-Performance Contouring Tool has six different edges to focus on different areas of your face. Long and medium smooth edges are made for classic lymphatic drainage, while shorter sides are ideal for areas around your eyes. The tool even includes rounded teeth for fine lines and a targeted tip for acupressure. (Face Gym has an instructional video to help guide you through all of this.)

Face Gym's gua sha tool is made from stainless steel, which is hypoallergenic and easy to clean. The stainless-steel tool is easy to clean, but any product can irritate skin. It also has a nice cooling effect after briefly popping it into the fridge. While this gua sha tool is on the pricier end, its stainless steel construction means it won't shatter like its crystal counterparts if you accidentally drop it.

Both are used for facial massage, but a roller moves across the skin by rolling, while gua sha uses sweeping strokes with a smooth-edged tool. You simply glide the roller across your face with gentle pressure to support lymphatic drainage. This is another stainless steel tool, which means it's a little more hygienic and easy to clean than its more traditional crystal versions. It's also highly likely to survive in the event of a drop.

The stainless steel has a natural cooling feel against the skin, although you can toss it in the fridge for extra chilliness. This tool is heavier than stone or crystal rollers—keep that on the back burner if you're used to those. It also pairs best with an oil or serum to help it glide smoothly over your skin, so plan to moisturize at the same time.

Dry brushing has the combined benefit of supporting lymphatic drainage and exfoliation at once. But some brushes have stiff bristles that can feel intense—and even irritating—against the skin. Esker's dry brush is gentle against the skin, but still feels firm enough to get things moving.

Esker's dry brush has a spa-like feel, along with an ergonomic design that's easy to grip. It's relatively petite, too, making it easy to toss in a bag for travel or trips to the gym. The only downside of that is the handle isn't long enough to reach your back. (That's more of an exfoliation issue vs. a lymphatic drainage problem, though.) The rules of lymphatic drainage still apply with a brush like this—if it feels irritating to your skin, stop. But if dry brushing is something you're into and you want to try lymphatic drainage on areas of your body other than your face, this is a solid choice.

Most people do gua sha on their face with a sculpting stone, crystal, or steel device. But not everyone is into the sensation of moving something hard across the sensitive skin in that area. Skin Gym answers the call with a face brush designed specifically for gua sha.

The brush is densely packed with soft bristles, creating a feel like you're swiping a really good makeup brush over your skin. It has an ergonomic shape, making it easy to glide over the contours of your face. This brush is pretty beginner-friendly, making it a good entry point if you're gua sha-curious. But be aware that you may not be able to get as much pressure on your skin (if that's even your thing) as you would with a stone or other hard tool. The brush also requires regular cleaning to avoid pushing dirt around your face.

Let's get this out of the way upfront: Vibration plates are a controversial tool. Many make bold claims, like that they can support weight loss or mimic the effects of exercise—those are unfounded. But these plates can improve circulation and lymphatic drainage as a result, as Rachelle Reed, PhD, an exercise scientist based in Athens, Georgia, previously told Women's Health.

FWIW, research suggests that you'll get many of the same circulation- (and lymph-)promoting effects from exercise. But if a vibrating plate is more your speed, the LifePro Waver is worth a look. This machine offers 99 speed levels to allow you to fine-tune the intensity. The motor is also quiet, so you don't have to stress about waking up other people in your home. This plate comes with resistance bands and free online workout videos, too. Just be aware that vibration plates aren't safe for everyone—you should take a pass if you're pregnant, prone to blood clots, or struggle with dizziness, for example. Bachelorette star Gabby Windey also recently shared that she broke her back after cranking up her (unnamed) vibrating plate in the name of lymphatic drainage. Though her account is an individual anecdote and doesn’t establish the typical risk, proceed with caution. But if you're looking for a way to get lymphatic drainage moving around your whole body, this is worth considering.

The best type of lymphatic drainage tool for you depends on where you plan to use it on your body. "These types of massages can be performed anywhere, but are extremely common on the face," Dr. Zeichner says. "Oftentimes, a smooth, but firm tool like gua sha is used."

A roller is another option for facial lymphatic drainage, and is usually considered more gentle than gua sha. For lymphatic drainage other than the face, some people reach for dry brushes and vibration plates.

For gua sha, Dr. Rodney suggests choosing a tool with smooth, rounded edges with no sharp spots, chips, or cracks. "It should be comfortable to hold and easy to clean," she says—and that applies to all lymphatic drainage tools. For gua sha and rollers, "you don't need an expensive crystal," Dr. Rodney says.

Dry brushes should also have natural fibers, since synthetic can feel harsh against the skin. Overall, "a smooth finish and gentle technique matter more than the price tag," Dr. Rodney says.

There's no exact weight for a lymphatic drainage tool that's best for everyone. Instead, it should feel substantial in your hand—but not too heavy or too light. You want to be able to comfortably use your tool, and allow the tool to apply pressure vs. heavy force from you.

They may temporarily reduce puffiness for some people, but evidence for at-home tools and broader health benefits is limited. "For everyday facial puffiness, gentle massage may offer temporary improvement," Dr. Rodney says. Dr. Zeichner agrees. "Especially if you wake up puffy in the morning after drinking too much alcohol, not having enough sleep, taking in too much salt, or during your menstrual cycle, lymphatic massages can be a useful tool," he says. Just keep in mind that the effects are temporary.

Every type of tool is slightly different. "The goal of a lymphatic massage is to improve the body's drainage system," Dr. Zeichner says. "That is why the massage should be performed in a particular way." If you're massaging your face, the pressure should start near the center of your face, before moving out and down toward your collarbones. This follows the natural lymphatic flow, Dr. Zeichner says.

"A few minutes is enough to start," Dr. Rodney says. "Keep the pressure light—bruising is a sign to stop, not a sign it’s working."

Dermatologists recommend taking a pass on lymphatic drainage tools if your skin is irritated, infected, sunburned, or broken. (That includes inflamed acne, eczema, or rosacea flares, per Dr. Rodney.)

Dr. Rodney also suggests checking with your doctor if you take blood thinners, bruise easily, or have blood clots, heart or kidney failure, lymphedema, or a history of cancer treatment or lymph node removal. "After cosmetic procedures or surgery, get clearance from your treating clinician," she says. "Persistent or painful swelling needs an explanation before it needs a massage."

#4887. South Korea Moves to Lift Its ICO Ban After Nearly a Decade

South Korea Moves to Lift Its ICO Ban After Nearly a Decade

South Korea is proposing to end its nine-year ban on initial coin offerings, a move aimed at pulling crypto fundraising back onshore, creating jobs and folding token sales into a regulated framework.

The country’s Financial Services Commission unveiled a draft bill, the Act on Digital Asset Industry Innovation and User Protection, on Tuesday that would reverse the prohibition imposed in September 2017, when regulators banned ICOs over fraud, speculation and investor losses.

If passed, it would let domestic projects issue and sell tokens to the public for the first time in nearly a decade.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Under the proposal, any issuer would have to file a “digital asset white paper” with the FSC before selling tokens, detailing the project, how the raised funds will be used, how many tokens will be issued and the risks involved. Issuers and their executives would face civil damages, financial penalties and possible criminal prosecution for false or omitted information, a liability regime modeled on the disclosure rules governing stock offerings.

The ban, regulators have concluded, never really worked. It largely pushed Korean projects to set up entities abroad and run their token sales through them, with game developers Wemade and Netmarble among the better-known firms that took the offshore route. The FSC’s stated goal is to reclaim that activity and the investment and jobs that went with it.

The ICO reversal is one piece of a sweeping overhaul. The same bill would restrict issuance of Korean won-backed stablecoins to consortiums in which commercial banks hold a majority stake, cap any single major shareholder’s ownership of a crypto exchange at 20% (rising to 34% under certain conditions), extend market-manipulation rules to crypto-to-crypto trades, and organize the market into regulated verticals spanning exchanges, trading, brokerage, custody and asset management.

The shift fits a broader global move toward regulated token fundraising, as the U.S. and others build out frameworks that give crypto issuers clearer legal footing. It also marks a notable turn for South Korea, one of the world’s most active retail crypto markets, which has long paired enthusiastic trading with strict rules.

The proposal is only a draft. It now heads to the National Assembly, where lawmakers must approve it before any of the changes take effect, leaving the timeline, and the final shape of the rules, still to be determined.

#4880. What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

The U.S. derivatives regulator has quietly opened the door for crypto exchanges and clearinghouses to hold Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins as part of the financial cushion they’re required to keep, the latest sign of the agency weaving digital assets into the plumbing of regulated markets.

But the fine print matters, and it draws a careful line.

In a staff advisory issued this week, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk explained how swap execution facilities, designated contract markets, and derivatives clearing organizations can use crypto assets to meet their financial-resources requirements.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Those rules require such platforms to hold enough resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs, a buffer meant to ensure a venue can keep running or wind down safely if it hits trouble.

Here’s what the guidance allows: Certain crypto assets, specifically naming Bitcoin, Ethereum, and payment stablecoins, can now count toward that 12-month requirement, subject to “appropriate haircuts,” meaning their value would be discounted to account for volatility. That’s a meaningful concession, effectively recognizing crypto as a legitimate corporate reserve asset for the firms the CFTC oversees.

Here’s what it doesn’t allow, and this is the catch that defines the policy: Crypto can’t be counted toward a separate liquidity requirement.

Because digital assets don’t qualify as “cash” or “highly liquid securities” under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, they fall short of that stricter test. In practice, a platform can hold Bitcoin or Ethereum as part of its longer-term financial backstop, but it still needs traditional cash-like instruments on hand to satisfy the rule meant to ensure it can pay obligations quickly.

The distinction is the whole point. It lets firms treat crypto as a store of value on their balance sheets while reinforcing that, when it comes to assets that must be instantly spendable, volatile tokens still don’t make the cut.

The nuance is easy to miss, but it reflects a measured posture from a regulator that has otherwise moved aggressively on crypto.

The CFTC has already previously cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, issued no-action relief letting crypto apps offer regulated derivatives, and floated a plan to bring crypto exchanges under federal oversight, part of a broader push to set digital-asset policy on its own authority.

That said, it’s worth noting that the advisory represents the views of CFTC staff only. It creates no new rules or enforceable rights, isn’t a no-action position, and doesn’t necessarily reflect the views of the Commission itself.

It could also shift as the agency’s makeup changes. President Donald Trump recently sent a bipartisan slate of nominees to fill vacant CFTC and SEC seats, which could reshape the commissions now steering crypto policy.

For now, the guidance is best read not as crypto winning blanket acceptance as a reserve asset, but as the CFTC sorting out precisely where digital assets fit, and where they still don’t, in the machinery of regulated trading.

According to the company’s disclosures, its payment services support more than 300 payment methods across 220 markets and process an average of over 20 million transactions daily.

#4876. Tennis is Aces for Healthy Aging

There’s good reason why the United States Tennis Association calls it “the world’s healthiest sport.”

If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research shows that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

“Tennis is a whole-body sport,” says sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”

You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin says.

And those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

When you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin says. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin says. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is important as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

Studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. #4875. Bitcoin Losses Are the Worst Since FTX. Is the Bottom Near?

Bitcoin Losses Are the Worst Since FTX. Is the Bottom Near?

Bitcoin investors are locking in their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX in November 2022, according to a report published Tuesday by blockchain analytics firm Glassnode.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency slipped below $60,000, trading at $59,992, more than 50% from its October 2025 peak.

“Bitcoin losses are the heaviest since FTX,” Glassnode wrote on X. “Set against the money that flowed into Bitcoin over the past year, they have almost doubled in a week.”

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Glassnode tracks realized losses by looking at coins that move on-chain at prices lower than when they previously moved. Measuring those losses against the capital that entered Bitcoin over the preceding year gives analysts a way to compare sell-offs across market cycles, even as the cryptocurrency grows in value.

The last time the indicator reached these levels, Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto empire was collapsing and Bitcoin was trading below $16,000. This time, the selling pressure has coincided with a much broader retreat from risky assets, and even good news for the tech industry hasn’t been enough to keep Bitcoin afloat.

Bitcoin rallied 5% in about half an hour on Monday after Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO. Less than six hours later, Bitcoin had given back the entire rally, while the Nasdaq 100 still held roughly three-quarters of its gains. In trading, this is known as a bull trap, and happens on strong bearish trends.

Bitcoin’s correlation with the Nasdaq 100 is now at its highest since September 2022, Glassnode said. Over the past 60 trading days, Bitcoin has tended to gain less when tech stocks rise and lose more when they fall.

U.S. investors have also been pulling money out of the market. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $4.3 billion on net over the past 20 trading days, while Coinbase traders have been heavy net sellers over the past month. Buying and selling on Binance, meanwhile, have been roughly balanced.

“Spikes like this often came close to past lows, but some came early,” Glassnode said. The firm pointed to the sell-offs of early 2019, March 2020, and November 2022, when losses surged near market bottoms, but also to earlier episodes in 2018 and 2022 when prices had further to fall.

Long-term holders—investors who have held their coins for roughly five months or longer—accounted for most realized losses from mid-April to mid-November. Nearly 90% of the long futures positions vulnerable to liquidation between last week’s Bitcoin price and $53,200 are also gone, reducing the potential for another cascade of forced selling within that range.

Glassnode is watching Bitcoin’s realized price, the average price at which circulating coins last moved, which currently stands at $53,200. Bitcoin traded below that metric before bottoming in each of the previous three major bear markets.

Applying the discounts seen at the lows of 2022 and 2018 to today’s realized price would put Bitcoin at roughly $41,000 and $37,000, respectively.

For now, the more immediate concern is whether Bitcoin can close above its June closing low of $58,500. Glassnode said a recovery above $60,000 accompanied by renewed ETF inflows would help establish whether the summer lows are holding.
