#4841. The 11 Best Deodorants for Women in 2026, Tested by a Beauty Editor

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Real talk: Deodorant isn't a sexy beauty product, but it's arguably one of the most important. Imagine plopping down on your exercise bike, pounding the pavement in your favorite running gear, or even just commuting to the office without one. Scary thought, right? Growing up in notoriously humid South Florida, I was always hyper-aware of body odor and well-acquainted with underarm sweat—and I knew that deodorant was the way to keep me dry and stink-free.

I've no doubt that one of the products below will get the job done beautifully for you (so please, scroll!). But here are a few expert pointers if you want to shop for the best deodorant on your own.

"Keeping underarms fresh involves two main goals: controlling sweat and eliminating B.O.," says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. That's where deodorants and antiperspirants come into play. The only problem? People often use the terms interchangeably, but they're actually very different.

Deodorants help mask or neutralize underarm odor caused by sweat mixing with skin bacteria, while antiperspirants use aluminum to reduce underarm sweat by blocking sweat glands, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. "One potential downside with antiperspirants is that they can dry out surrounding skin, leading to irritation, itching, and rash for those with sensitive skin," adds Alicia Zalka, MD, a dermatologist and associate clinical professor at Yale University School of Medicine.

Controlling sweat and masking bad odors are both important, but you'll have to be honest to decide which is a higher priority for your needs. If you're a heavy sweater and want to stop underarm wetness, opt for antiperspirants. If excess perspiration isn't as big of an issue for you, stick with deodorants. My daily go-to is deodorant, but I swiped both types to share the full scoop on the best women's deodorants and antiperspirants in the game. And the best part? Everything starts at just $9.

You've probably seen a variety of deodorant and antiperspirant formulations, and Dr. Murphy-Rose says your choice should be based upon personal preference and your unique issues. That said, there are some differences between the different types, so here's a quick rundown to think about.

Solids and sticks typically have a waxy consistency, are generally well-tolerated, and usually are the best for sensitive skin. Dragging on the skin is usually the primary source of irritation with these, so "try warming the stick on your skin first before swiping to minimize friction," advises Dr. Murphy-Rose. They also tend to leave behind annoying powdery white streaks on dark clothes and stickiness on the underarm area, adds Dr. Zalka. (All of these featured solids and sticks did not leave behind any residue on my clothes.)

Gels are convenient roll-ons and are typically light or clear so naturally, they leave behind less residue than solids. The only downside is that they tend to feel wet on skin—so if you're already dealing with excess perspiration, you may not love that sensation.

Creams feel moisturizing and soothing with application, but are a bit more messy and not as easy to apply. They're totally worth using, especially if you're looking to concentrate the application to a specific area or want full-body coverage (think between skin folds or under your breasts). Creams are typically more hydrating than gels and are a good option for those prone to dryness or irritation, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Spray deodorants are quick to use, lightweight, and typically fast-drying, so they're practical for days you're in a rush. "They feel light and dry quickly with fewer ingredients," says Dr. Zalka. However, some may contain alcohol, which can be dehydrating or irritating for sensitive skin. Sprays can also be messy because you can't fully control where all of the deodorant particles land.

In general, you'll want to use deodorants made with moisturizing ingredients like humectants like hyaluronic acid or glycerin for hydration and occlusives like shea butter or beeswax to help protect dry, itchy underarms, recommends board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD. There are also deodorants made with bentonite clay, powders, or baking soda to help combat moisture. Important to note: "None of these ingredients blocks sweat ducts—they work by absorbing moisture," she says. Dr. Murphy-Rose is also keen on deodorants made with low concentrations of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) to minimize underarm discoloration and baking soda.

That's slightly different from antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts to stop perspiration by creating plugs that block sweat glands, using aluminum, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. She adds that most over-the-counter antiperspirants contain 12 to 25 percent aluminum, while prescription-strength formulas can go up to about 30 percent.

I'm our resident scent-obsessed beauty editor and have tried a slew of deodorants and antiperspirants throughout my nearly decade-long journalism career. For this story, I kept the above dermatologist-approved guidance in mind and carefully researched hundreds of women's deodorants and antiperspirants.

Next, I went to the Women's Health beauty closet and revisited products in my personal collection until I eventually narrowed down my list to 24 potential contenders that seemed promising. I tested these deodorants after showering and, on weekends spent indoors, I delayed showering my underarms to see how these products held up against smell and sweat. I also considered how much odor and sweat protection they provide while exercising, running errands across New York City, and wearing them on special occasions and nights out with friends.

I also considered their ease of use, how they feel on my underarms, whether they leave behind any residue (a major pet peeve of mine), and how frequently I needed to apply to remain confident in how I smell.

With that, I give you: the best women's deodorants of 2026. They are all loved by me, and some are even well-known among the dermatologists I spoke with for this story. Regardless of which deodorant you order, they all earned major snaps from me, a very hard-to-please beauty editor. The best part? They all start at just $9 and don’t leave behind embarrassing white marks on clothing. Sign me up for bulk orders!

When it comes to selecting the best overall deodorant for women, it's tough to find a winner that doesn't include aluminum. As mentioned above, aluminum is the only active ingredient approved to stop perspiration in its tracks—a major consideration. What's more, the powdery texture works double duty to absorb moisture and leave skin with a silky finish.

And like most Dove products, this stick is chock full of moisturizing ingredients so you can rest assured that this one won't dry out your skin. “I feel like this is a deodorant you can’t go wrong with," says Women's Health beauty writer Danielle Jackson. "I recently switched back to this after using some aluminum-free formulas with more subtle scents, and I’ve just found that I’m much more confident about any sort of odors being blocked when I wear it."

But the ultimate test is, Can this hold up to activity? Jackson says this Dove stick passes that test with flying colors. "I also realized that I don’t have to worry as much about it doing its job when I’m being active or working out," she says. "It lasts all day and has a powdery scent that smells great but isn’t overbearing.”

When it comes to usage, Jackson assures that the Dove antiperspirant stick glides on easily without pulling (a major downside for most other sticks) and won't leave any white marks on my skin or clothes. Talk about an A+!The one potential downside (if you can even call it that) is that some of the other products on our list have a longer-lasting dryness promise (this one will only keep you dry for 24 hours as opposed to, say, the 48 or 72 hours promised by some other brands). But if you're like me and shower frequently, that won't be an issue.Read more: Best Natural Deodorants

A Women's Health Beauty Award winner for best deodorant, this heavy-duty antiperspirant leaves me with fresher-smelling pits from the second I swipe and up to 48 hours later. Obviously, I'm not going two days without showering, but I do notice that whenever I wear this antiperspirant while enjoying HIIT exercises or on the treadmill I'm less sweaty. Now that's pretty amazing.

Secret swears their antiperspirant helps camouflage sweat caused by activity, nerves, and heat—and I think it does a solid job, especially for heat. I wore this deo regularly back when I practiced martial arts, swam, rode horses, and attempted to play tennis. I don't normally sweat heavily, but in the summer I'd definitely reach for this antiperspirant especially when commuting underground on the New York subway system. It’s still helpful during the fall and winter season when I’m bundled up in several layers.

The only thing I don't enjoy about Secret is the packaging design. It's shaped like your standard stick deodorant where I twist the bottom to help push up the creamy formula, but I noticed the turn mechanism on mine requires a little more effort than others on this list. But if you're a heavy sweater, that's a fairly minor downside—and you shouldn't let this small con deter you from this one.

I learned about this deodorant years ago through my mom, who has been using Tom's forever. I tried it during the pandemic, but stopped using it in favor of other deodorants. But, I wanted to revisit Tom's for this story—and I'm so glad that I did.

The brand recently reformulated their line of natural deodorants, and I'm obsessed with the chic new packaging and all the incredible new scents available, like Wild Lavender, North Woods, and Mountain Spring. Tom's swears the formula is still as long-lasting as ever though, with this deodorant keeping odor at bay for 48 hours. That's pretty impressive for a natural formula. Like I said earlier, I won't ever skip my daily shower (occasionally twice daily in the summer because it's that humid along the East Coast) but Tom's keeps up with my daily activities. Think long daily commutes to the office, full workdays, after work shenanigans, and so much more.

To be frank, this level of protection isn't the norm for natural deodorants, but this stick is formulated with a generous dose of glycerin and aloe to condition my skin. It's also free of artificial fragrances that can irritate sensitive noses like mine.

All this being said, this is not the formula for you if you're a heavy sweater. I'd also say the biggest bummer about this deodorant is that it doesn't glide as easily as other alternatives on this list. There's a light dragging on my underarms, but it's not a huge problem, rather a minor annoyance that shouldn't deter you from enjoying this pick.

Is anyone else flashing back to middle and high school gym class just looking at this deodorant? I know I am, but there are several reasons every girl in my PE classes all used this roll-on antiperspirant—it's so easy to use and it's virtually invisible.

Since it's an antiperspirant, Ban keeps me sweat- and odor-free and embarrassing sweat marks on my clothes are nonexistent when I roll this onto my underarms (its clear formula doesn't transfer or leave behind any marks). What I really appreciate about Ban, though, is how it's lightweight on my skin. Sometimes creamy sticks feel like they're leaving behind a clump of product onto my pits, but that's a non-issue with Ban.

One important thing to note is that this gel roll-on doesn't dry quickly. It's not a huge drawback—the waiting period is minimal—but if you're in a super rush in the morning, keep that in mind. It's also not quite as long-lasting as some of the other formulas at 24 hours, but that's not a problem for me since, again, I shower daily.

I've always preferred stick deodorants and antiperspirants because it's what I'm used to. But this Dove formula makes a compelling case for anyone who's also shopping for weightless odor and sweat protection. So how does it work? “They create a flexible film of active ingredients on your skin and remain dry,” says cosmetic chemist Perry Romanowski. Dove relies on finely milled aluminum for invisible protection, plus a special masking oil to prevent any marks from getting on my clothes.

But similar to spray sunscreens, spray deodorants and antiperspirants can get a little messy and feel hard to control, and this one is no exception. So, it's probably best to skip buying this one for someone who isn’t super clean or a preteen who might spray this a little too liberally.

As we've said before: Whole body deodorants are hugely popular right now, with all the major players getting in on this trend. It's a smart idea—just 2 percent of our sweat glands exist in our underarms, so it's clear the need for all-over odor solutions is great.

This formula, with tapioca starch and mandelic acid, works to acidify skin’s pH, preventing odor-causing bacteria from proliferating. Rub a pea-sized amount into smelly areas, including the vulva, under-boob, thigh folds, and underneath the butt cheeks. A little goes a long way here, and you can always add more as needed.

Since its launch, Lume has expanded its portfolio to include stick deodorants, wipes, body creams, body washes, and acidified cleansing bars that are pH-optimized to control odor.

You deserve a deodorant that can keep up with your active lifestyle. Who better than tennis star Sloane Stephens to create a high-performance natural whole B.O.dy deodorant. I’m a huge fan of this spray and previously named it one of the best whole body deodorants of all time.

What impresses me the most is that 24/7 Hustle is made with clean ingredients, but it doesn’t skimp on performance or irritate my skin. I wore it from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m., and was pleasantly surprised that I still smelled fresh and felt clean throughout a long travel day. It keeps up with light and intense physical activity. When I want to touch up I just swiftly spritz on this spray and I’m good to go after workout classes. No obvious residue or clammy coating that sticks to my workout sets. Woo!

So how does it work? The proprietary Deoplex Complex contains enzymes that help neutralize BO, while a botanical blend of goji berry, dragon fruit, chamomile, and ashwagandha prevents environmental damage that causes dry skin. The gentle formula also soothes my sensitive skin.

A bonus: This is the only refillable deodorant worth your hard-earned money. You can purchase a refillable pouch with enough liquid to refill your bottle nearly three times for $35. The combined price of a single refill pouch and the initial bottle is $53, while purchasing four new bottles would cost $72, resulting in a savings of nearly $20.

Dermatologist Kiran Mian, MD, previously called this one of the best natural deodorants out there because of its impressive ingredients. "It has a blend of probiotics, plant-based extracts, antioxidants, cornstarch for moisture absorption, and soothing ingredients to prevent irritation," Dr. Mian said. It’s also infused with hyaluronic acid to help hydrate my sensitive underarm skin without feeling damp throughout the day.

This is one of the best natural deodorants I’ve used in the last two years. The odor protection is comparable to traditional deodorants even during workouts and unairconditioned subway rides around New York. It definitely keeps up with sweltering summer weather along the East Coast and Euro vacations with ease.

Other reasons I’m a huge fan? It doesn’t leave behind a white cast on my clothing and it holds up nicely after exercising. Since I’m not a runner, I can’t vouch for its efficacy there, but I will say it quite literally has me covered during vinyasa yoga and mat pilates. This deodorant also holds up surprisingly well on the StairMaster and high incline walks on the treadmill.

I’m not the only fan. Tester Brigitt Earley is impressed by the texture of this deodorant, which she describes as almost like a body butter in stick form—and I agree. It doesn’t skip or tug on my skin, which has been an issue with other competitors.

Truly, the only downside with this deodorant is the price but I will say each one easily lasts me at least two months. Technically, I’m only paying $10 a month to have stink-free underarms and that’s well worth the cost to me.

If you’re familiar with any of my skincare content at Women’s Health then chances are you’ve likely seen me gush about Nécessaire products. I’m a ride-or-die fan of the brand’s body wash, exfoliator, serum, and deodorant. The line’s genius lies in the simple yet effective ingredient list. Think odor-neutralizing mandelic acid (an alpha-hydroxy acid) paired with triethyl citrate and zinc ricinoleate for odor-protection. The soft and creamy stick deodorant is also infused with soothing vitamin B3, B5, and E for hydration.Another reason I’m genuinely obsessed with this deodorant? The incredible variety of enticing scents that are noticeable enough for me to enjoy but wouldn’t overwhelm my colleagues at work.

The featured Hinoki scent is my top pick—and the one I crowned as the winner in our 2025 Skincare Awards package. Inspired by Japanese hinoki cedar trees, this earthy and woody aroma is a zen dream. It also blends notes of basil, vetiver, and magnolia, adding a spa-like serenity to my morning routine.

Another reason I love this deodorant is that it glides on seamlessly without dragging my sensitive pits. It also doesn’t leave behind white marks on my dark clothing.

TBH, it was super hard to brainstorm a true con. Nécessaire gets so many things right with this formulation. They even have a gel deodorant if that’s more your vibe. If I’m forced to name one area of improvement then it would be that there aren’t any travel-sized versions. The cylinder shape does take up a decent amount of space in my cosmetic pouch, but TBH, the formula and longevity are worth it for me. Still, if you’re a seasoned traveler who keeps things minimal, then you should consider the Anti Odorant pads instead.

Meet my favorite deodorant launch of 2026. I recently crowned it the best deodorant of the year in our annual Beauty Awards package. Here’s the TL;DR: They’re travel-friendly wipes that can be used all over the body.And now that the weather has finally warmed up, I’m heavily relying on these dermatologist-developed deodorant wipes to help me win the battle against body odor.

Their genius lies in the trifecta of odor-neutralizing enzymes, soothing aloe vera juice, and exfoliating glycolic acids that don’t sting or tingle my sensitive skin. I’ve tried the spray and love it, but the wipes are my current go-to. Since they’re individually wrapped, I can keep a few in my gym bag, work tote, and carry-on bag so my pits are quite literally covered.

TBH, I genuinely enjoy these deodorant wipes, which is why they took home a big win. However, if I must be nitpicky then it would be cool if these were available in multiple scents. However, that might easily irritate very sensitive skin types and those with sensitive noses. And honestly, the current mild scent isn’t bad—just natural and fresh, which I appreciate. Plus, it won’t accidentally clash with my perfume collection.

I've spent four years wearing this deodorant on and off and can confirm that evolvetogether hits all of the factors I look for in a deodorant. For starters, it’s made with natural ingredients. Instead of potentially harsh baking soda, aluminum, and talc, this deodorant uses tapioca starch to soak up sweat and moisture. There's also DeoPlex, a plant-based sugarcane that neutralizes bad odors, while glycerin moisturizes and prevents underarm irritation. Panthenol hydrates my underarms and helps the stick glide on easily.

Most importantly, the odor protection is on point! If you are from the South like I am then you know that even if we shad our underarms sometimes it's so hot and humid out that we inevitably get a little smelly. Not the case with evolvetogether. I've worn this deodorant walking 5Ks around my neighborhood, on the treadmill, during long cross-country flights, and I've never felt self-conscious about my smell. (My mom is also very honest and would have told me if I ever have an odor issue, so I know evolvetogether works well for me.)

As for the cons, it’s really minimal. Heavy sweaters like runners will likely need a traditional antiperspirant to keep their pits truly dry. However, for daily activities this is one of my long-time favorites.

Look, there are studies that have investigated potential links between aluminum-based antiperspirants and breast cancer or Alzheimer’s disease. "To date, no conclusive evidence supports these claims, and aluminum-based antiperspirants are generally considered safe for daily use. There is no clear evidence that they pose a significant health risk," says Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Want more proof? Well, the American Cancer Society says "there are no strong epidemiologic studies (studies in people) that link breast cancer risk and antiperspirant use, and very little scientific evidence to support this claim." Plus, this report in the National Library of Medicine details a study conducted on 130 people regarding the potential exposure to aluminum through antiperspirants, antacids, and Alzheimer's disease (AD). "For all antiperspirant/deodorant use, regardless of aluminum content, there was no association with AD,” according to the study.

#4839. The Kids Are Outside: The Rise of the Adult Children’s ADU

When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home. And while Sam is thriving professionally as a sales rep with his own place, they never expected that his house would be in their backyard. But the nightmarish Bay Area real estate market made a 400-square-foot ADU (accessory dwelling unit) on his parents’ property, complete with a separate entrance and direct street access, seem like the best option for the 32-year-old. “It was becoming difficult for him to afford rent while also saving toward eventually buying a place of his own,” Diane tells AD. “He’s close by, but it really feels like he has his own home.”

While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.

Diane and Steve Weaver on their property’s ADU

Blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis. These days a homebuyer needs an annual income between $110,000 and $113,000—well above the national average income of $64,220 per year—to comfortably afford a median-priced home in the US, which is currently priced at $434,900. While this has led some grown kids to move back into their childhood bedrooms, in cases where acreage allows, families like the Weavers are opting to be neighbors instead of housemates by setting up self-contained living spaces on the same lot as their single-family homes. In California, they’re certainly no outlier. The state has passed legislation specifically encouraging the construction of ADUs to address the housing shortage—which resulted in quadruple the number of ADU permits issued in the Golden State from 2017 to 2022.

Those in the ADU construction game say families like the Weavers make up an increasingly large slice of their business. Jeremy Nova, co-founder of the Colorado-based prefab ADU builder Studio Home, says ADUs for adult children are popular among his clients because the arrangement is mutually beneficial. The kids are afforded some independence and the ability to save money, “while for the parents, it can also be a long-term investment. The same space that houses an adult child today could eventually become a rental or a separate living space for a caregiver.” ADU builders on the opposite coast are seeing the same demand. Justin Olewack, president of Bolt Builders, says that ADUs for adult children are becoming a top request among his clientele in the DC, Virginia, and Maryland areas, where housing costs have risen 61 percent since 2016.

If it cuts costs and results in a sellable amenity down the line, perhaps moving back home isn’t the failure-to-launch scenario it was once seen as.

An ADU by Studio Home, built in the backyard of a Scottsdale, Arizona, family’s property.

Once a family’s adult child moves out of the property’s ADU, especially if it has a kitchen and bathroom, the structure can serve as a rental, providing passive income for retired parents. Tracy Noh, who hired John Brennan of BZBuild Co to build her daughter Eliza Bowen an ADU in Burbank, was thinking long-term with her compound planning. “An in-home apartment would require sharing the space of our 1,000-square-foot main home. And, as someone who works from home, the ADU seemed a better solution,” she says.

Noh and Eliza show off their Burbank ADU.

The living arrangement has also enabled Noh and her daughter to develop their own life paths. The structure gives her daughter a space in which she can become a young adult, and Noh the opportunity to step back from making the day-to-day household decisions. The former is learning how to manage her own household: planning meals, budgeting expenses, and making time for household chores.

“That change in dynamic also allows us both to remain much calmer in our interactions with each other,” Noh says. It’s not just because there’s a separate place for each of them to retreat to; Noh says she has “gained an enormous amount of respect for Eliza and her ability to manage her own home. It’s a fabulous opportunity to begin to build that adult-to-adult relationship with your child.”

The interior of Tracy Noh’s ADU by BZBuild Co

While modest ADUs serve single occupants just fine, more sizable ADUs allow a family’s adult children to bring their own kids in tow. Oren Amir, co-founder of SoCal builder GO Home Builders, points out that in his experience, the catalyst for aging parents to build an ADU for their adult children is almost never just the adult child themselves: It’s the grandchild they will be bringing with them. “The call comes a few months before or after a baby arrives,” he says. The grandparents don’t want to travel to visit their grandkids; they want them living nearby. Rent in Los Angeles is what stops people from saving, and early parenthood is when saving matters most, Amir says. An ADU in a grandparent’s backyard, therefore, lets the adult children stay in the neighborhood, raise the baby near help, and set some money aside for when the time comes to leave the nest for good. “Everyone gets what they need and nobody has to move in,” Amir says of the arrangement.

While the Weaver family ADU is Sam’s for now, it could grow up to be a granny flat someday. “It’s possible that Sam might live in the main house and we could move into the ADU as we age,” says Diane. “It gives us a lot of options for how the space can be used as our family’s needs change.”

#4835. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

Francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a new installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the big screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” says Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”

Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

Though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a new stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

“I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” says Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”

Haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

The stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety shows, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The New York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

Production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch says.

To recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence says of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”

While District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the new location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

“Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

In the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

“It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

The upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

The Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence says, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

The set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch says. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”

The library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch says. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

The aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I said there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”

Designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”

Lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance

Seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” says Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

Despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson says. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”

#4829. In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage

“I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” says Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires—a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity.

Cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in New York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” says Cooney.

Cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market.

Cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts.

“We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” says Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates.

The husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods, while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” says the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it

Cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it.

Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques.

“It’s the diva of the project,” says Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s New White.

The kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island.

The saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs.

“The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” says Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.”

The architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones.

To expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench.

A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” says Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print.

Cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt. Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce.

Making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagined the space, like painting existing wainscoting in Farrow & Ball’s Tanner’s Brown, and covering the walls in a botanical House of Hackney Herbarium wallpaper. For a touch of texture, Cooney also layered vintage rugs and set an antique Victorian bamboo chair in the corner below the window.

With a view over the living room, Cooney says the lofted floor is like a little escape within the small cottage. Leaning into the cozy feel, the team went with a layered look. A brass chest anchors the space, paired with a black armchair owned by the clients, which was reupholstered with a burgundy fabric from Abraham Moon & Sons, and a Lawson-Fenning Morro Sectional in a linen blend.

The clients’ only real hesitation was a bit of a surprise: the reclaimed brick Cooney specified for the mudroom. It is laid in a herringbone pattern with colors that appeared to shift across the surface. That yellow kitchen? Totally fine. But the expressive bricks? Too dramatic. “We relied on the team’s judgement, and this feature is now one of our most favorite parts of the home,” says the husband, noting how guests often compliment the mudroom.

“I feel like this house is kind of us unchecked,” says Cooney of her clients’ trust. “No one checked us, so we were allowed to do the fullest extent of what we wanted to do.” Her clients could easily have staged their own diva moment after the cabinets were painted in screaming yellow, before everything else around it fell into place around it; but they let the vision come into full focus.

As if cantilevered over the hill, a screened-in porch is the best of both worlds. “You don’t have to have everything be indoor-outdoor in a covered porch—you can really pull the inside out there and not worry so much,” says Cooney, nodding to choices like Henning Kjaernulf dining chairs from the 1960s purchased from Lone Fox. And while most might use a lighter color in this space, Cooney chose a deeper Farrow & Ball Hopper Head paint for the walls and window frames, which she says helps punctuate the view in a beautiful way.

#4828. The 8 Best Home Office Chairs, Approved by Spine Specialists

The best seats for boosting productivity and evading back pain.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you work from home, you know how much of a difference the right office chair can make. Take it from someone who's spent five years working remotely and learned the hard way that the couch isn't the best place to spend a workday. Between a standing desk, an under-desk treadmill, and monitors, outfitting your home office can get expensive. But if you're going to splurge on one piece of WFH gear, an ergonomic office chair that supports your back throughout the workday is a good place to start.

“A supportive chair can reduce the risk of lower back pain, neck and upper back pain, poor circulation, and fatigue,” says Kevin Lees, director of chiropractic operations at The Joint Chiropractic. “This may also lead to improved productivity, enabling individuals to stay focused on their tasks without distractions from trying to get comfortable.”

To find the best home office chairs, our team consulted spine specialists and tested several popular ergonomic chairs for weeks in our own workspaces, sitting for up to eight hours a day. Our favorite is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, which impressed us with its customizable support and easy assembly at a reasonable price compared to premium models from Herman Miller and Steelcase.

The right home office chair will be different for everyone, but there are a lot of factors that will remain the same, like adjustable lumbar support and thick seat cushioning. Keep reading to find which of these eight expert-recommended chairs are the perfect addition to your workday.

Meet the experts: Kevin Lees, Director of Chiropractic Operations at The Joint Chiropractic.Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care.

The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our pick for the best home office chair because of its combination of comfort, adjustability, and value. At $499, it’s packed with easy-to-use adjustments that make it a steal. You can customize the seat depth, lumbar support, tilt tension, recline, and more without having to take your eyes away from your work.

After testing the chair for over a month and sitting for four to six hours per workday, WH Digital Designer Taryn Colbert gave it a five out of five, praising how easy it was to assemble and customize. In fact, she found herself using it even when she wasn't working.

“While I work, I sit it up to work on my posture,” she says. When doing her hair or playing computer games, she reclines the chair into what she calls “lounge mode.”

The armrests alone offer five types of adjustment, and you can add a headrest or a taller cylinder for an additional cost. While the mesh version has a low-key look, the leather and vegan leather options are worth considering if you want a bit more style.

Colbert’s biggest gripe was the wide wheelbase, which made it difficult to maneuver through doorways and across carpet.

Still, if you’re looking for a classic ergonomic office chair, this model is great for both first-timers and seasoned remote workers. Its customizable design is intuitive enough to use every day without requiring a four-figure investment.

From the iconic Eames Lounge Chair to the ergonomic Aeron office chair, Herman Miller has earned its reputation for making some of the best seats around. At upwards of $1,500, the Aeron is certainly an investment, but you can customize practically everything, from the arm pads to the casters. It’s available in three sizes, with several options for armrest adjustability, back support, and tilt.

WH Deputy Editor Eunice Lucero-Lee tested the medium-size Aeron in the Jasper colorway for two to four weeks, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. Lucero-Lee, who regularly experiences lower back pain, gave the chair a 5 out of 5.

“This had perfect lumbar support for a whole eight-hour day's work,” she says. She also appreciated the adjustable armrests and how smoothly and quietly the wheels rolled while still offering enough traction and control. (The deep forest green colorway was another bonus.)

Instead of a traditional foam cushion, the Aeron features a breathable mesh seat that offers an almost weightless feeling. And the chair arrives fully assembled—as we'd expect at this price point.

While the steep price tag was Lucero-Lee’s biggest gripe, the Aeron’s customizable fit and excellent lumbar support make it a worthwhile splurge if you spend the better part of your day at your desk.

If you like to lean back and stretch your legs between meetings, the FlexiSpot ErgoX is worth checking out. Beyond customizable lumbar support, seat depth, and armrests, it features an adjustable headrest and a retractable footrest, so you can kick back and put your feet up while catching up on emails or taking a breather between calls.

WH Fitness Reviews Editor Natascha Grief, who already owns a Herman Miller office chair, tested the ErgoX for over a month, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. While she initially found the back support a little uncomfortable, it took about a week for her to get used to sitting in a more upright position.

“I think a good comparison would be switching to a pair of very supportive/corrective shoes after wearing pairs that are less structured,” she says. Once she adjusted to the chair, she liked the firm back support and how the headrest helped her maintain a comfortable neck position.

Grief also loved how comfortable the chair was when fully reclined, though she found the mechanism for pulling out the footrest a little clunky. She ultimately gave the chair a 4 out of 5.

Considering how many adjustments and extras you're getting for the price, the ErgoX is a great option if you prefer a more supportive seat but still want the flexibility to kick back throughout the workday.

Like the Herman Miller Aeron, the Steelcase Gesture comes at a luxury price point, but its sturdy construction, supportive cushioning, and impressive range of adjustments help justify the investment. The chair comes in different materials and colors. Plus you can customize wheels for hard floors or carpet.

Of its many adjustable features, including recline and lumbar support, the most unique is its 360-degree armrests, which allow you to comfortably position your arms whether you're typing on your laptop or scrolling through your phone.

After testing the Gesture for two to four weeks and sitting for two to four hours per workday, WH Managing Editor Laura McLaughlin gave it a 5 out of 5. She loved the firm seat cushion and how the chair managed to feel both stable and flexible.

“The back support specifically feels incredible, with firm yet comfortable padding and adjustable lumbar support,” she says.

At nearly 60 pounds, the chair is on the heavier side, and McLaughlin found it surprisingly difficult to roll around. That said, she felt that its weight contributed to how sturdy and supportive it was.

The Gesture can also support up to 400 pounds, just like the Steelcase Series 2, and is backed by a 12-year warranty, which is reassuring when you're spending four figures on an office chair.

If preserving your home’s interior design is top of mind, then the Branch Verve is minimalist with a unique flair and very comfortable. Made by the same brand as our top pick, this chair is $100 more and has fewer points of adjustment, but it also has a thick seat cushion and a breathable, beautifully designed 3D-knit back that comes in seven chic monochromatic looks.

You can adjust lumbar support, seat depth, and tilt for a decent fit. The chair comes with an optional headrest for $59 more, and the armrests are height-adjustable as well as removable. The chair itself is on the heavier side, weighing in at 40 pounds, but it’s also Greenguard Gold certified, which means it has been tested for volatile organic compounds and chemical emissions.

Read More: Best Standing Desks For Walking Pads

For those who struggle with back pain, a supportive office chair can be the difference between a productive workday and injury. The Steelcase Series 2 is the best option for those folks because it’s weight-activated—you just sit, and the chair’s back tension adjusts to you.

The thick seat cushion relieves pressure, and you can adjust the height, width, and depth of the armrests. (Most office chair armrests are just adjustable by height and sometimes width.) The chair can also support up to 400 pounds, which is about 100 pounds more than most of our picks. In terms of design, you can choose between a variety of colors, two frame colors, an optional headrest, and wheels for carpet or hard flooring.

Read More: Uplift Kneeling Ergonomic Chair Review

At under $500, the HON Ignition 2.0 is a budget office chair that still delivers in terms of support and adjustability. The chair itself is lightweight and easy to maneuver at under 25 pounds, and it sports a simple silhouette that won’t be an eyesore in your home office. The armrests can be raised and widened, and you can also easily adjust lumbar, tilt, and seat depth.

You can also opt to forgo armrests to bring the price closer to $400 or add a headrest and still keep the chair under the $600 threshold. The chair also comes backed by a limited lifetime warranty, which is unique for a high-quality home office chair. (For reference, the warranty on our top pick only lasts for seven years.)

At less than $100, the TikTok-famous Pukami Criss Cross Chair is a great option if you’re furnishing your home office on a budget. The extra-wide, foam-cushioned seat offers plenty of room to sit cross-legged, and its minimalist design and variety of color options make it easy to match with your home decor.

Despite its affordable price tag, the chair swivels, tilts, and can support up to 350 pounds. While it lacks the adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and wheels of our pricier picks, it’s worth considering if you work from home occasionally and don’t want to spend hundreds of dollars on an office chair.

Here are some key features to consider while you search for the best office chair for your body and needs.

Office chairs are not one-size-fits-all, which is why adjustability is crucial. “Adjustability lets the chair match your body so your spine stays in a neutral, supported position,” says Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care. The lumbar support should match the curve of your spine, and your feet should be able to sit flat on the floor, according to Okubadejo.

“An unsupportive chair, or one that does not fit properly, can lead to chronic musculoskeletal injuries over time,” Lees says. “This may lead to pain that persists throughout the day, affecting sleep and stress levels. Long-term injuries may also include nerve damage that can lead to weakness or numbness.”

Most home office chairs are height adjustable and have armrests that can be raised. If a chair has a headrest, which isn’t essential, that may be adjustable as well. “Being able to tweak depth, tilt, and lumbar support prevents hot spots and improves blood flow during long sits.” Okubadejo says. “Small adjustments through the day break up static strain, so muscles don’t fatigue and posture doesn’t collapse.”

Lumbar refers to the lower back, and supporting this curve in your spine can relieve disc pressure and keep your pelvis in a neutral position, according to Okubadejo. “Good lumbar support lowers the risk of stiffness and pain during long hours at a desk,” he says.

Like chair height and seat cushioning, lumbar support will vary by person. “Postural muscles start to relax after a few minutes of sitting,” Lees says. “This leads to added stress on the spinal joints and extremity joints.” Luckily, many office chairs allow you to adjust the height and curve of the lumbar support. Okubadejo recommends options that can move up and down as well as in and out instead of stationary lumbar support.

The main components of a comfortable office chair are a sturdy frame, a thick seat cushion, and a supportive, breathable back. Most office chairs these days have a metal or plastic frame with a foam cushion and mesh back, although you can find upholstered and leather versions.

If you have the opportunity to test chairs in person, make sure that the seat is firm enough for you. “If the cushion is too soft, it won’t offer the support needed over time,” Lees says. “A cushion that is too firm could create pressure points and possibly affect blood flow in the legs.”

The materials of a chair can contribute to its overall weight and weight limit—both of which are important to keep in mind during your search.

Office chairs, like our top pick from Branch, can be beautiful in their own right but not necessarily as stylish as a sofa or armchair. Unfortunately, you may need to prioritize comfort over design when working from home, but you can opt for chairs with upholstery-like materials or lots of color options to marry the two.

Office chairs range in price from under $100 to more than $2,000, but you’ll find that most quality office chairs will cost around $500. It may seem like a lot to spend on a single chair, but it may also be your most-used piece of furniture outside of your bed and mattress if you work from home.

As a longtime remote worker and someone who suffers from chronic back pain, I’m particularly passionate about high-quality office chairs. When I set out to find the best home office chairs, I looked for a variety of models that would suit different body types, from height to weight. Supportive office chairs are easily adjustable, especially when it comes to seat height, armrest height, and lumbar support, so I wanted to highlight chairs that delivered on all three and beyond, with a few budget-friendly exceptions.

My top picks span a wide range of prices, from just $60 to a couple of luxury investment options over $1,500. Whether you’re starting a new remote job or desperately need to revamp your home office, these are the best home office chairs that will keep you comfortable and supported all day long.

#4825. Mauviel's Copper Cookware Is 25% Off For Black Friday

There are a few covetable luxury goods you’ll see pop up again and again in AD’s home tours: a Moccamaster coffee maker, a Nordic Knots rug, and Mauviel copper cookware, to name a few. As seen in this Sag Harbor home, this Parisian pied-à-terre, this Westchester residence, and this Connecticut country retreat, Mauviel is something of a status symbol in kitchens. Much like a Le Creuset Dutch oven out on display, spying a few copper pans from the French brand hanging from a rail signals that “Great Taste Lives Here.” And this week marks a good opportunity to join the club, with Mauviel sets and individual pieces up to 30% off for Black Friday at Williams Sonoma and on Shop.

I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast. Of course it does. Unlike some of my ceramic pans that catch and dry out an egg, the Mauviel has given me no trouble, delivering me the most perfect eggs to date I’ve ever cooked. Even against my stainless-steel pans (which I do love very much), these heat a bit more quickly and evenly.

That excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple. Mauviel has made copper cookware since 1830 in Villedieu-les-Poêles, a town in Normandy with an enduring history of copper manufacturing; the pieces are still handcrafted there. As far as their makeup, the M’150 B pieces are, for example, 1.5 millimeters thick and constructed of a 90% polished copper exterior and a 10% stainless-steel interior. They heat evenly; are immediately responsive to heat adjustments; and work on gas, electric, and ceramic cooktops.

The pans partners with a copper kettle on the stove in this Portland manse by Jessica Helgerson.

The copper treasures do, however, require care. They’re not nonstick pots and pans, so you need a little oil or butter to get any slip. They’re hand-wash only, and Mauviel advises against using them for long stretches on high heat or leaving them empty on a hot burner. I don’t polish mine, simply because I don’t own any copper polish. The wear shows quickly, and I like that, though if AD were shooting my house, maybe I’d like it less.

The Black Friday markdowns run across the line: my copper fry pan is going for $280 in the 10-inch size (25% off), a 2.5-quart sauce pan is $450 (29% off), and a 15-piece cookware set is $3,000 (32% off). For anyone who cooks every day, it’s a hard gift to beat. I, for one, now can’t imagine frying my eggs any other way.
